sources.title: A. Marks, Set Theory (Berkeley lecture notes, revised 2026-01-31; complete 106-page set)
sources.locator: Sections 3-9, printed pp. 15-42 (Wellorderings; Ordinals; Transfinite induction and recursion on ordinals; Induction and recursion on wellfounded relations; The cumulative hierarchy; The axiom of choice; Cardinality in ZF), read in full

contents.name: Section 3, definition of wellfounded and wellordered strict partial orders (p. 15)
Exercise 3.1 (suborderings of wellfounded orders are wellfounded)
contents.reason: A transfer result for suborderings; no item of this pair uses subordering transfer, and the examples work with the least-element property directly.

contents.name: Lemma 3.2 (an order-preserving self-map of a wellfounded order never moves downward, f(a) is not below a)
Lemma 3.3 (the identity is the only isomorphism of a wellordering onto itself)
Corollary 3.4 (isomorphic wellorderings have a unique isomorphism)
Lemma 3.5 (no wellordering is isomorphic to an initial segment of itself)
Lemma 3.6 (comparability of wellorderings, with uniqueness of the witness)
Remark 3.7 (setlike wellorderings of classes)
contents.reason: Recursion along class-length wellorders; it belongs with the class-recursion rule that ordinal arithmetic is built on, not with the set-sized recursion proved on this page.

contents.name: Definition 4.3 (ordinal: a transitive set well ordered by membership)
Exercise 4.1 (x is transitive iff every element of x is a subset of x)
Exercise 4.2 (unions and intersections of transitive sets are transitive)
Lemma 4.4 (if alpha is a proper subset of beta then alpha is a member of beta)
Lemma 4.5 (an element of an ordinal is an ordinal and an initial segment)
Lemma 4.6 (two ordinals are comparable under inclusion)
Corollary 4.7 (membership linearly orders the ordinals)
Lemma 4.8 and Definition 4.9 (every nonempty class of ordinals has a least element; inf)
Lemma 4.10 (every set of ordinals has an upper bound, its union)
Definitions 4.11, 4.14 (sup of a set of ordinals; sequences of ordinals)
contents.reason: The supremum operation and ordinal-length sequences are the vocabulary of ordinal arithmetic; the present page forms only unions and sets of order types.

contents.name: Exercise 4.12 (alpha is the set of ordinals below it; intersections of classes; unions of sets; alpha+1 as inf of the ordinals above alpha)
Exercise 4.13.1 (the class of all ordinals is not a set)
Exercise 4.13.2 (the class of countable ordinals is a set)
Lemma 4.15 and Definition 4.16 (every wellordering is isomorphic to a unique ordinal; order type ot)
Definition 4.17, Lemma 4.18, Lemma 4.19 (successor alpha+1, it is an ordinal, and beta < alpha+1 iff beta <= alpha)
Definition 4.20 and Lemma 4.21 (omega and mathematical induction)
Lemma 4.22 and Lemma 4.23 (every natural number is an ordinal; omega is an ordinal)
Theorem 5.1 and Exercise 5.2 (transfinite induction in the three-case and single-hypothesis forms)
Theorem 5.3 (transfinite recursion on ORD for a class function)
contents.reason: Recursion along the whole class of ordinals; the set-sized schema on this page is published, while the class rule is the prerequisite of the next page's ordinal operations.

contents.name: Definition 5.4 and Lemma 5.5 (ordinal addition and the order type of alpha disjoint-union beta)
contents.reason: Ordinal addition is the subject of the next ordinal page; this pair deliberately introduces no ordinal operation beyond successor and union.

contents.name: Definition 5.8 (ordinal multiplication)
contents.reason: Ordinal multiplication belongs to the ordinal-arithmetic page, which is the declared destination for the whole operation block.

contents.name: Exercise 5.9 (alpha times beta is the lexicographic order on alpha x beta)
contents.reason: The general product identity is proved by transfinite recursion on the ordinals; only its omega x omega instance, which needs no ordinal product, is used here.

contents.name: Definition 5.12 (ordinal exponentiation)
contents.reason: Ordinal exponentiation belongs to the ordinal-arithmetic page and no item of this pair uses it.

contents.name: Theorems 5.20 and 5.21 (Goodstein sequences are terminating but this is unprovable in Peano arithmetic)
contents.reason: Independence results for Goodstein sequences are far beyond this pair and are promised by no page of the plan; the recursion theorem they use is already published here.

contents.name: Section 6 (induction and recursion on wellfounded relations; the rank of a set)
Section 7 (the cumulative hierarchy V_alpha and rank)
contents.reason: The cumulative hierarchy and rank belong to the planned well-founded-relations page, where rank is developed for arbitrary well-founded relations.

contents.name: Theorem 8.4 (Zermelo's wellordering theorem)
Section 8, equivalences of AC, Zorn's lemma and the wellordering theorem
Definition 9.1 and Exercise 9.2 (same cardinality; injections versus surjections)
Theorem 9.3 (Cantor-Schroeder-Bernstein in ZF)
Definition 9.4 (cardinal; omega_alpha; aleph_alpha; omega_1 is the least uncountable ordinal)
The aleph enumeration omega_alpha and Exercise 9.5 (behaviour at limit ordinals)
contents.reason: The aleph hierarchy and its continuity at limits are promised by the cardinal-arithmetic page, which also owns cofinality.

contents.name: Theorem 9.6 (Hartogs' theorem) and the Hartogs number h(X)
Definition 9.7 and Theorem 9.8 (the cardinal successor kappa+ and Cantor's theorem)
contents.reason: Successor cardinals and Cantor's theorem about power sets are the opening results of the cardinal-arithmetic page.

contents.name: Definitions 9.9-9.11 and Lemma 9.12 (cardinal arithmetic; |alpha x alpha| = |alpha| for infinite alpha)
contents.reason: Cardinal arithmetic is promised by the cardinal-arithmetic page; the present pair uses only the ordinal definition of a cardinal.

sources.title: J. T. Moore, MATH 6870: Set Theory (Cornell lecture notes; complete set)
sources.locator: Sections 3-8, printed pp. 6-22 (Classes, Ordinals, and Transfinite Induction; Well Founded Relations and Transfinite Recursion; Ordinal arithmetic; Applications of transfinite recursion; Cardinals and Cardinality; The Axiom of Choice), read in full

contents.name: Theorem 3.1 (no set is an element of itself, from Foundation)
Definition of transitive set and of ordinal (a transitive set well ordered by membership)
Theorem 3.2 (an element of an ordinal is an ordinal)
Theorem 3.3 (trichotomy for ordinals)
Successor and limit ordinals; Axiom of Infinity; omega is the least limit ordinal
Corollary 3.4 (Burali-Forti: the class of all ordinals is not a set)
Theorem 3.5 (transfinite induction: a nonempty class of ordinals has a least element)
Theorem 4.1 (transfinite recursion for set-like well-founded relations)
contents.reason: The general well-founded-relation recursion is a stronger theorem than the well-order recursion published here; it is promised by the planned well-founded-relations page.

contents.name: Lemmas 4.2 and 4.3 (transitive R-closure; every nonempty class has an R-minimal element)
contents.reason: Transitive closures and class minimality for arbitrary well-founded relations belong to the planned well-founded-relations page.

contents.name: Theorem 4.4 (recursion on ON)
contents.reason: Class-length recursion on the ordinals is the tool of the ordinal-arithmetic page, where the recursion rule is stated and used.

contents.name: Section 5 (ordinal addition, multiplication, exponentiation, Cantor normal form; 1+omega = omega < omega+1)
contents.reason: Ordinal arithmetic and its normal form are the declared content of the ordinal-arithmetic page; this pair uses no ordinal operation.

contents.name: Corollary 6.1 (Mostowski collapse of a well-founded relation to a transitive set)
contents.reason: The collapse for arbitrary well-founded extensional relations is promised by the planned well-founded-relations page; the well-order case is published here.

contents.name: Corollary 6.2 (a well ordered set is isomorphic to a unique ordinal; order type)
Corollary 6.3 (given two well orders, one is uniquely isomorphic to an initial segment of the other)
Corollary 6.4 (the rank function of a well-founded set-like relation)
contents.reason: Rank functions for well-founded relations are promised by the planned well-founded-relations page; the failure of the recursion without well-foundedness is recorded here as a counterexample.

contents.name: Theorem 6.6 (Hartog ordinal: a least ordinal that does not inject into a given set)
Theorem 7.2 (Cantor-Schroeder-Bernstein)
Theorem 7.3 (Cantor: no surjection from x onto its power set)
Corollaries 7.4 and 7.5 (cardinal comparability implies the well ordering principle)
contents.reason: Cardinal comparability and its choice strength are the subject of the cardinal-arithmetic and cofinality page.

contents.name: Cardinals are initial ordinals; the finite cardinals are exactly the elements of omega; omega+1, omega*omega and omega^omega+1 are not cardinals
The aleph hierarchy omega_alpha
contents.reason: The aleph hierarchy is defined on the cardinal-arithmetic page; this pair computes only the Hartogs number of finite sets and of omega.

contents.name: Section 8 (the Axiom of Choice, its equivalences and Zorn's lemma)

canonical.name: The finite von Neumann ordinals and omega = union omega, without any choice principle
The falsity of 'the ordinals form a set' as a recorded refutation
The falsity of 'transfinite induction and recursion need the Axiom of Choice' as a recorded refutation
The proved choice ledger for well-orders, cardinals, Hartogs and the basis theorems

Definition 4.3 with Lemma 4.8 (an ordinal is a transitive set well ordered by membership; members of ordinals are ordinals)
Exercise 4.12 and Definition 4.17 (alpha is the set of ordinals below it; successors)
Lemma 4.15 and Definition 4.16 (order type) instantiated at a finite chain

Section 6 (recursion requires well-foundedness) instantiated at Z with its usual order
Theorem 9.6 (Hartogs' theorem) instantiated at a finite set
Theorem 9.6 (Hartogs' theorem) instantiated at omega, with the countable ordinals forming a set
Theorem 5.1 and Exercise 5.2 (transfinite induction) at omega with the least element exempted
Section 3, wellordering of Z by an explicit formula (0, 1, -1, 2, -2, ...)
Section 5, Exercise 5.9 and the remark that lexicographic orders on Z x Z are not wellorders

canonical.name: Boundary case: the set {0,1,omega} of ordinals is not transitive, hence not an ordinal
Boundary case: a lexicographic order on Z x Z is total but has a nonempty subset with no least element
Boundary case: the shift x -> x+1 is a nonidentity order automorphism of (Z,<), and x -> x-1 moves every point down
Boundary case: the collapsing equation F(a) = {F(b) : b < a} has no solution on (Z,<)
